rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary wished for death either before the ordeal or before this event, from modesty, fear of blame, or concern that people might sin by speaking about her.
rows.anchor: استحياء من الناس وخوفا من لائمتهم أو حذرا من وقوع الناس في المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Mary heard a call, ‘Come out, O worshipper of other than God,’ and grieved and wished for death.
rows.anchor: وروي أنها سمعت نداء أخرج يا من يعبد من دون الله تعالى فحزنت لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wishing for death in such a religious crisis is unobjectionable; wishing for it because of worldly pain or hardship is disliked, as a Muslim report instructs one to leave the choice to God.
rows.anchor: نعم يكره تمنيه لضرر نزل به من مرض أو فاقة أو محنة من عدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is a grave misjudgment to say Mary wished for death because labor pain was severe.
rows.anchor: ومن ظن أن تمنيها عليها السلام ذلك كان لشدة الوجع فقد أساء الظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nasiy means an insignificant thing liable to be forgotten and disregarded, such as a menstrual rag; the description reflects conventional usage even of what is not literally forgotten.
rows.anchor: أي شيئا تافها شأنه أن ينسى ولا يعتد به أصلا كخرقة الطمث

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Most readers have kasra in nasiy; al-Farraʾ treats kasra and fatḥ as two dialect forms and prefers fatḥ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأكثرون ( نسيا ) بالكسر قال الفراء : هما لغتان في ذلك كالوتر والوتر والفتح أحب إلي

rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī says kasra is the more elevated of the two language forms.
rows.anchor: وقال الفارسي : الكسر أعلى اللغتين

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī analyzes kasra as the noun for something forgotten and fatḥ as a verbal noun used in place of that noun.
rows.anchor: هو بالكسر اسم لما ينسى كالنقض اسم لما ينقض وبالفتح مصدر نائب عن الاسم

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي؛ نوف الأعرابي؛ بكر بن حبيب السهمي
rows.claim: Reported readings include nasʾa with hamza and kasra, nasʾa with hamza and fatḥ, and, in Ibn ʿAṭiyya's report, nasā without hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ محمد بن كعب القرظي ( نسئا ) بكسر النون والهمزة مكان الياء وهي قراءة نوف الأعرابي

rows.speaker: الأعمش؛ أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash and Abū Jaʿfar in one transmission read the mīm of mansiy with kasra by vowel assimilation, as in other assimilated forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وأبو جعفر في رواية بكسر الميم اتباعا لحركة السين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس؛ نوف
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Nawf identify the caller as Gabriel; ʿAlqama's reading substitutes ‘addressed her,’ which Abū Ḥayyān also takes to mean Gabriel.
rows.anchor: أي جبريل عليه السلام كما روي عن ابن عباس ونوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘From below her’ can mean a physically lower place; al-Ḥasan says Gabriel stood on a lower patch, perhaps out of reverence for Mary.
rows.anchor: وكان في بقعة من الأرض أخفض من البقعة التي كانت عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Gabriel stood beneath Mary to receive the child is improper because it attributes an unworthy act to the trusted angel of revelation.
rows.anchor: والقول بأنه عليه السلام كان تحتها يقبل الولد مما لا ينبغي أن يقال

rows.speaker: أبو حيان؛ مجاهد؛ وهب؛ ابن جبير؛ ابن جرير؛ ابن زيد؛ الجبائي
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers Jesus as the caller, with ‘below her’ referring to Mary: God made the newborn speak; this is reported from several early authorities.
rows.anchor: واستظهر أبو حيان كون المنادى عيسى عليه السلام والضمير لمريم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس؛ الحسن؛ الجبائي؛ مجاهد؛ وهب؛ ابن جبير؛ ابن جرير؛ ابن زيد
rows.claim: The alternative caller-Jesus interpretation is transmitted from Mujāhid, Wahb, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Zayd, al-Jubbāʾī, and, through al-Ṭabrisī, al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: وروي ذلك عن مجاهد ووهب وابن جبير وابن جرير وابن زيد والجبائي

rows.speaker: قراء الابنان والأبوان وعاصم والجحدري وابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: These readers open the mīm of man, making it a relative pronoun and subject of ‘called’; it can mean either Jesus or Gabriel.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الابنان والأبوان وعاصم والجحدري وابن عباس والحسن في رواية عنهما ( من ) بفتح الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Do not grieve’ can be parsed with explanatory anna or with an elided preposition before a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: على أن أن مفسرة أو بأن لا تحزني على أنها مصدرية قد حذف عنها الجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking ‘beneath you’ as ‘under your command’ is possible but departs from the apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: وقيل : تحت أمرك إن أمرت بالجري جري وإن أمرت بالإمساك أمسك وهو خلاف الظاهر

rows.speaker: البراء؛ الحاكم
rows.claim: Al-Ḥākim transmits from al-Barāʾ that sari means a stream and grades the report sound according to the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections; al-Bukhārī cites it suspended, while connected versions are mawqūf, not soundly raised to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أي جدولا كما أخرجه الحاكم في مستدركه عن البراء وقال : إنه صحيح على شرط الشيخين

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd's verse uses sari for a watercourse and is cited as lexical evidence for that meaning.
rows.anchor: فتوسطا عرض السرى فصدعا مسجورة متجاوزا قلامها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A verse cited by Ibn ʿAbbās compares a generous person's bounty to a stream fed by rivers, illustrating sari as a channel.
rows.anchor: سهل الخليقة ما وجد ذو نائل مثل السرى تمده الأنهار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report identifies the stream as a channel from the Jordan that God caused to flow when Mary was thirsty.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك على ما روي عن ابن عباس جدولا من الأردن أجراه الله تعالى منه لما أصابها العطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports say Gabriel struck the ground and a fresh spring flowed, or Jesus caused it, as transmitted from Abū Jaʿfar; another view says it was already there and God pointed it out.
rows.anchor: وقيل : فعل ذلك عيسى عليه السلام وهو المروي عن أبي جعفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stream newly produced by a miracle best fits the passage's emphasis on extraordinary signs and its apparent wording.
rows.anchor: وما تقدم هو الموافق لمقام بيان ظهور الخوارق والمتبادر من النظم الكريم

rows.speaker: الحسن؛ ابن زيد؛ الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Zayd, and al-Jubbāʾī take sari to mean Jesus, a boy of exalted rank, deriving it from elevation rather than flowing water.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن وابن زيد والجبائي أن المراد بالسري عيسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Lord's provision explains why Mary need not grieve; calling God ‘your Lord’ and attaching the pronoun to her dignifies and reassures her.
rows.anchor: والجملة تعليل لانتفاء الحزن المفهوم من النهي عنه والتعرض لعنوان الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Huzzi ilayki means ‘shake toward your direction’; shaking may be forceful or gentle, and ilayki is explained by taking the verb as containing the sense of inclination.
rows.anchor: أي إلى جهتك والهز تحريك يمينا وشمالا سواء كان بعنف أو لا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān objects to attaching ilayki to huzzi: Arabic grammar does not let a verb take a second attached object matching its raised attached pronoun, outside specified verb classes.
rows.anchor: ومنع أبو حيان تعلقه بهزي وعلل ذلك بأنه قد تقرر في النحو أن الفعل لا يعدى إلى الضمير المتصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān supports the restriction with parallel examples such as ‘I looked toward you, and Zayd looked,’ where the second phrase cannot mean he looked toward himself.
rows.anchor: والضمير المجرور عندهم كالضمير المنصوب فلا يقال : نظرت إليك وزيد نظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line places ʿalayka after a verb with a raised pronoun, and grammarians treat ʿalā there as a noun; another cited line has ‘from above it.’
rows.anchor: ومن هنا جعلوا على في قوله : هو عليك فإن الأمور بكف الإله مقاديرها اسما

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān makes ilayki depend on an omitted explanatory word, while Ibn Mālik and al-Qāmūs limit explanatory ilā to contexts that signal love, hatred, or a superlative, absent here.
rows.anchor: وجعل الجار والمجرور هنا متعلقا بمحذوف أي أعني إليك

rows.speaker: ابن عصفور؛ ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṣfūr reports Ibn al-Anbārī's claim that ilā can be a noun, as in ‘I went from toward you,’ which would remove Abū Ḥayyān's objection.
rows.anchor: حكى ابن عصفور في شرح أبيات الإيضاح عن ابن الأنباري أن إلى تستعمل اسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making ilā mean ‘at’ or treating it as a verbal particle does not yield a convincing sense here; the proposed noun analysis also conflicts with Abū Ḥayyān's claim of consensus on its prepositional status.
rows.anchor: ولعلها حينئذ بمعنى عند فقد صرح بمجيئها بهذا المعنى في القاموس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers understanding huzzi as containing the sense ‘incline,’ with ilayki attached to that sense; this is a distant but defensible resolution.
rows.anchor: والذي أميل إليه في دفع الإشكال أن الفعل مضمن معنى الميل والجار والمجرور متعلق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He questions whether the grammatical prohibition is sound in practice, since constructions such as ‘hold your wife to yourself’ and several Arabic examples exhibit the pattern; converting all examples is strained.
rows.anchor: على أن في القلب من عدم صحة نحو هذا التركيب للقاعدة المذكورة شيئا لكثرة مجيء ذلك في كلامهم

rows.speaker: ذو الرمة
rows.claim: Dhū al-Rumma's line ‘if you excuse yourself for lack of water’ illustrates huzzi used as an intransitive verb, so the bāʾ marks the means or instrument.
rows.anchor: فإن تعتذر بالمحل من ذي ضروعها إلى الضيف يجرح في عراقيبها نصلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in bi-jidhʿ is instrumental, as in writing with a pen; making the object an omitted fruit, rutab, or a circumstantial phrase is strained, and the first analysis best fits the unusual wording.
rows.anchor: فالباء للآلة كما في كتبت بالقلم

rows.speaker: المبرد؛ أبو حيان؛ الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad's proposal that rutab is the object by verb competition is rejected because shaking falls on the trunk and the word is separated from its verb; al-Farrāʾ's claim that hazzahu and hazz bihi are synonyms is also dismissed.
rows.anchor: وعن المبرد أن مفعوله ( رطبا ) الآتي والكلام من باب التنازع

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited line about free women ‘not reading the surahs’ is offered as a parallel for an allegedly emphatic extra bāʾ, a proposal the author does not prefer.
rows.anchor: هن الحرائر لأربات أخمرة سود المحاجر لا يقرأن بالسور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī's Kashf is invoked in favor of the first, instrumental analysis as the one that suits the Qur'an's unusual expression.
rows.anchor: والوجه الصحيح الملائم لما عليه التنزيل من غرابة التظم كما في الكشف هو الأول

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poetic line comparing a reed-like canal reddened with blood is cited as an example of feminine agreement for a noun whose gender comes from its annexed noun.
rows.anchor: كما شرقت صدر القناة من الدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding alternative analysis of the feminine pronoun is sound but contrary to the apparent reading.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأنه خلاف الظاهر وإن صح

rows.speaker: مسروق؛ أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Masrūq and Abū Ḥaywa have readings with feminine tāʾ, sukūn of the sīn, and kasra of the qāf; another transmission has yāʾ instead of tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مسروق وأبو حيوة في رواية ( تسقط ) بالتاء من فوق مضمومة وكسر القاف

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa also reads with open tāʾ and ḍamma on qāf, and transmits the corresponding yāʾ reading; rutaban is then a specification or, in one report, a nominative subject.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا كذلك إلا أنه بالياء من تحت فنصب ( رطبا ) على التمييز

rows.speaker: أبو السمال؛ البراء بن عازب؛ الجمهور
rows.claim: Abū al-Sammāl reads with two tāʾs, al-Barāʾ with yāʾ from asāqiṭu, and the majority with tasāqaṭu; rutaban is accusative as a specification in these readings.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال ( تتساقط ) بتاءين وقرأ البراء بن عازب ( يساقط ) بالياء من تحت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readings permit rutaban as a circumstantial accusative; masculine agreement points to the trunk, feminine to the palm or the feminine referent already explained.
rows.anchor: وجوز في بعض القراآت أن يكون على الحالية الموطئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Janiyy means freshly picked and ready for harvest, with faʿīl used in the passive sense; the lexicon also defines it as fruit picked just now, hence a laudatory description.
rows.anchor: أي مجنيا ففعيل بمعنى مفعول أي صالحا للاجتناء وفي القاموس ثمر جنى جنى من ساعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes janiyy as active, meaning fresh and fully ripened; Ṭalḥa reads it with kasra of the jīm by vowel assimilation, while Ibn al-Sayyid would expect feminine janiya, a suggestion the author questions.
rows.anchor: وقيل فعيل بمعنى فاعل أي رطبا طريا وكان المراد على ما قيل إنه تم نضجه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports a miraculous instant growth: the palm had neither trunk nor crown, but after Mary shook it shoots, spadix, green dates, red dates, and ripe fruit appeared at once.
rows.anchor: لم يكن للنخلة جذع ولم يكن لها رأس فلما هزته إذ السعف قد طلع

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله؛ أبو روق
rows.claim: The dates are said to have been barni, or ʿajwa according to Abū ʿAbd Allāh; Abū Rawq reports that bananas accompanied them, though the apparent reading mentions only dates.
rows.anchor: وكان برنيا وقيل عجوة وهو المروي عن أبي عبد الله

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Bāqir says nothing benefits a postpartum woman like dates and cites God's provision of them to Mary; a report also pairs dates for postpartum recovery with honey for the ill.
rows.anchor: فعن الباقر رضي الله تعالى عنه لم تستشف النفساء بمثل الرطب إن الله تعالى أطعمه مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to shake indicates that seeking one's provision is generally required and does not contradict reliance on God; a poem says every matter has its means even though God could make the palm bend unaided.
rows.anchor: وفي أمرها بالهز إشارة إلى أن السعي في تحصيل الرزق في الجملة مطلوب وهو لا ينافي التوكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary eats the dates and drinks the stream; another view makes the drink date juice, so drinking does not prove that sari means a watercourse.
rows.anchor: فكلي ( من ذلك الرطب ( واشربي ( من ذلك السرى وقيل : من عصير الرطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage arranges provision as water, food, eating, then drinking; explanations include water's greater immediate need, cleansing and broad benefit, its visible flow, and the customary order of eating before drinking.
rows.anchor: من إحضار الماء أولا والطعام ثانيا ثم الأكل ثالثا والشرب رابعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says water is basic and broadly useful, more visibly dispels sorrow, while eating is placed before drinking by ordinary custom or to sit beside ‘whatever you wish’—the dates.
rows.anchor: وقيل : قدم الماء لأنه أصل في النفع ونفعه عام للتنظيف ونحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commands to eat and drink may be obligatory, recommended according to Mary's circumstance, or merely permissive.
rows.anchor: والأمر قد يحتمل الوجوب والندب وذلك باعتبار حالها وقيل هو للإباحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarri ʿaynan means be at peace and let go of grief; the expression can derive from the eye becoming still at a pleasing sight or from the cool tears of joy, contrasted with hot tears of sorrow.
rows.anchor: وطيبي نفسا وارفضي عنها ما أحزنك

rows.speaker: قراء نجد
rows.claim: Najd readers pronounce the qāf of qarri with kasra; their dialect opens the past-tense eye vowel and uses kasra in the present, unlike other speakers.
rows.anchor: وقريء بكسر القاف وهي لغة نجد وهم يفتحون عين الماضي ويكسرون عين المضارع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stream and ripe dates console Mary through two extraordinary signs that show God's power can clear her name beyond ordinary expectations; grief can otherwise keep a person from eating or drinking.
rows.anchor: وتسليتها عليها السلام بما تضمنته الآية من إجراء الماء وإخراج الرطب من حيث أنهما أمران خارقان للعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If sari means Jesus as a high-ranking child, the stream still consoles her by showing that God has honored her; both the words and events vindicate her.
rows.anchor: ومن فسر السرى برفيع الشأن سامي القدر جعل التسلية بإخراج الرطب

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd reports that Jesus told Mary not to grieve; she feared the lack of a husband or master as an excuse before people, and Jesus promised to handle the speech.
rows.anchor: وقد يؤيد هذا في الجملة بما روي عن ابن زيد قال :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘If you see any human’ means any human being at all.
rows.anchor: أي آدميا كائنا من كان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the hamza substitution as a dialect like labbaʾtu bi-l-ḥajj and ḥallaʾtu al-sawīq, where hamza and the weak letters are interchangeable.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري : إنه من لغة من يقول لبأت بالحج وحلأت السويق

rows.speaker: طلحة؛ أبو جعفر؛ شيبة
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa, Abū Jaʿfar, and Shayba read tarayni with still yāʾ and light nūn; Ibn Jinnī calls it anomalous because the jussive should drop the nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة وأبو جعفر وشيبة ( ترين ) بسكون الياء وفتح النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary's instruction to say the vow indicates that she should explain herself if questioned.
rows.anchor: فقولي ( له إن استنطقك ( إني نذرت للرحمن صوما

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي؛ أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī reads ṣiyāman, and ʿAnas reads ṣamtan as in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh; the intended sense is silence, which may be a literal subset of fasting or a figurative use.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنه ( صياما ) والمعنى واحد أي صمتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the vow meant abstaining both from ordinary fast-breakers and from speech, a devotional practice in earlier law that Islam later prohibited, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ states.
rows.anchor: المراد به الصوم عن المفطرات المعلومة وعن الكلام وكانوا لا يتكلمون في صيامهم

rows.speaker: ابن قدامة؛ القفال
rows.claim: Ibn Qudāma says silence-vows are not Islamic practice and apparent reports prohibit them, so they need not be fulfilled; schools agree, while al-Qaffāl hesitated over the earlier-law practice.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الأخبار تحريمه فإن نذره لا يلزمه الوفاء به ولا خلاف فيه بين الشافعية والحنفية

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr tells a woman who vowed silence that Islam has annulled this practice and she should speak.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه دخل على امرأة قد نذرت أن لا تتكلم فقال :

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود؛ حارثة بن مضرب
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masʿūd via Ḥāritha b. Muḍarrib recounts his rebuke of a man who vowed not to speak: Maryam used silence to excuse herself from suspicion of illicit birth, but the man should speak and enjoin right.
rows.anchor: عن حارثة بن مضرب قال : كنت عند ابن مسعود فجاء رجلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ṣawm means silence, Maryam's statement either excludes only speech beyond the explanation of her vow or reports the wording of that vow; one group says she was to explain it by gesture, which is the stronger view.
rows.anchor: وقال فرقة : أمرت أن تخبر بنذرها بالإشارة قيل : وهو الأظهر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says Arabs call any communication reaching a person kalām unless it is emphatically specified as speech, supporting an explanation by gesture.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : العرب تسمي كل ما وصل إلى الإنسان كلاما بأي طريق وصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her restriction to an insī rather than any person implies she could speak to an angel or address God; she was told to avoid disputing with fools and let Jesus provide decisive proof.
rows.anchor: أن المراد فلن أكلم اليوم إنسيا وإنما أكلم الملك وأناجي ربي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس؛ سعيد بن منصور؛ ابن عساكر
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Mary came to her people carrying Jesus after forty days, when her postpartum bleeding had ended; she may have longed for home and trusted God to resolve matters.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا المجيء على ما أخرج سعيد بن منصور وابن عساكر عن ابن عباس بعد أربعين يوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says people searched for Mary, questioned Zechariah, accused him, and followed a bird's call to the tree; when she saw them she carried the child to meet them.
rows.anchor: فسألوا يوسف عنها فقال : لا علم لي بها وإن مفتاح باب محرابها عند زكريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent verse and reports say Mary came with the child without being summoned; another report says the people sent for her after learning of the birth.
rows.anchor: فظاهر الآية والأخبار أنها جاءتهم به من غير طلب منهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses fariyy as something enormous; another explanation calls it astonishing.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : عظيما وقيل : عجيبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fariyy is connected to cutting hide for repair or damage; the author prefers the triliteral derivation because faʿīl is regularly formed from triliteral roots.
rows.anchor: وأصله من فري الجلد قطعه على وجه الإصلاح أو الإفساد وقيل : من أفراه كذلك

rows.speaker: الكسائي؛ الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Rāghib distinguish farā as cutting for repair from afrā as cutting for corruption; al-Baḥr says the word can describe great good or evil, in word or deed.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح عن الكسائي أن الفرى القطع على وجه الإصلاح والإفراء على وجه الإفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may treat shayʾan as a direct object or as an absolute object meaning ‘you have come with an astonishing coming’; calling it ‘a thing’ heightens the shock.
rows.anchor: ونصب ( شيئا ) على أنه مفعول به وقيل على أنه مفعول مطلق أي لقد جئت مجيئا عجيبا

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa reads fariyy with sukūn on the rāʾ according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya; Ibn Khālawayh reports his hamza reading faraʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة فيما نقل ابن عطية ( فريا ) بسكون الراء وفيما نقل ابن خالويه ( فرأ ) بالهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Sister of Aaron’ renews the accusation and intensifies the rebuke; the Aaron meant is not Moses' brother, as the Prophetic report explains that people were named after earlier prophets and righteous people.
rows.anchor: استئناف لتجديد التعبير وتأكيد التوبيخ وليس المراد بهرون أخا موسى بن عمران

rows.speaker: المغيرة بن شعبة؛ رسول الله
rows.claim: In the report about the people of Najrān, the Prophet explains that they named people after prophets and righteous predecessors; this answers the objection that Moses preceded Jesus by centuries.
rows.anchor: بل هو على ما روي عن الكلبي أخ لها من أبيها

rows.speaker: الكلبي؛ قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says Aaron was Mary's paternal brother; Qatāda instead calls him a righteous Israelite, and reports that forty thousand Israelites attended his funeral, sharing his name.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبد الرزاق وعبد بن حميد عن قتادة قال : هو رجل صالح في بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr identifies a wicked Aaron whom the people invoked to insult Mary; another view means Moses' brother, transmitted from al-Suddī and ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن سعيد بن جبير أنه رجل طالح فشبهوها شتما لها

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī also says Aaron can name his descendants collectively, as with a tribal name, so Mary was one of them and ‘sister’ indicates membership.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون هرون مطلقا على نسله كهاشم وتميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appeal to Mary's parents either establishes the enormity of her alleged act or points out that offspring from righteous roots are generally expected to be wholesome, making deviation more blameworthy.
rows.anchor: تقرير لكون ما جاءت به فريا أو تنبيه على أن ارتكاب الفواحش من أولاد الصالحين أفحش

rows.speaker: عمر بن بجاء التيمي
rows.claim: The poet ʿUmar b. Bajāʾ reads mā kāna abāki imruʾu sawʾ, making the predicate definite and subject indefinite; the possessive gives the latter a slight license.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر بن بجاء التيمي الشاعر الذي كان يهاجي جريرا ( ما كان أباك امرؤ سوء )

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Mary points to Jesus so they will question him; the apparent reading is that she explained her vow by gesture, as commanded, rather than by speech.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنها بينت حينئذ نذرها وأنها بمعزل من محاورة الإنس حسبما أمرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports say the people called her gesture more insulting than the alleged sexual sin; the author explicitly disavows this charge against her.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار أنها لما أشارت إليه كلموه قالوا : استخفافها بنا أشد من زناها وحاشاها

rows.speaker: قتادة؛ عكرمة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses the cradle as the mother's bosom; ʿIkrima says it is the swing, with other views identifying a cot or resting place.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : المهد حجر أمه وقال عكرمة : المرباة أي المرجحة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: To explain the past tense kan, al-Zamakhsharī says it marks an indefinite past narrowed by the context to yesterday: how can they question one who was just in the cradle? The relative pronoun stresses continued infancy.
rows.anchor: أن كان الإيقاع مضمون لجملة في زمان ماض مبهم يصلح لقريبه وبعيده وهو ههنا لقريبه خاصة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: His second analysis takes the clause as a depiction of past circumstances and man as descriptive: they have never questioned a cradle child before, and the present form vividly portrays persistence.
rows.anchor: أن يكون ( نكلم ) حكاية حال ماضية ومن موصوفة والمعنى كيف نكلم الموصوفين بأنهم في المهد

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda treats kāna as an emphatic extra and ṣabiyyan as an intensifying circumstantial phrase; the author rejects Ibn al-Anbārī's objection that an extra kāna cannot govern its predicate.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة : كان زائدة لمجرد التأكيد من غير دلالة على الزمان

rows.speaker: السيرافي
rows.claim: Even grammarians who say extra kāna still indicates a past temporal frame do not solve the difficulty by that analysis.
rows.anchor: وعلى قول من قال : إن كان الزائدة لا تدل على حدث لكنها تدل على زمان ماض

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says man is best taken as a conditional pronoun, not a relative or descriptive one; the author says the resulting interpretation is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : الأجود أن تكون من شرطية لا موصولة ولا موصوفة أي من كان في المهد فكيف نكلمه ولا يخفى بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus' speech answers an implied question about what happened; he is reported to have stopped nursing, turned toward the people, leaned left, pointed, and spoken, while another account says Zechariah prompted him.
rows.anchor: روي أنه عليه السلام كان يرضع فلما سمع ما قالوا ترك الرضاع وأقبل عليهم بوجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus begins by declaring himself God's servant because acknowledging servanthood is the first spiritual station and directly refutes those who claim divinity.
rows.anchor: وذكر عبوديته لله تعالى أولا لأن الاعتراف بذلك على ما قيل أول مقامات السالكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything Jesus says indirectly establishes Mary's innocence and honors her: God would not choose an illegitimate child, a premise the people themselves accepted.
rows.anchor: وفي جميع ما قال تنبيه على براءة أمه لدلالته على الاصطفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Authorities differ whether Jesus spoke normally after this miracle or fell silent until the usual age of speech; his inclusion among cradle speakers favors silence in the intervening years.
rows.anchor: واختلف في أنه بعد أن تكلم بما ذكر هل بقي يتكلم كعادة الرجال أو لم يتكلم حتى بلغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book given to Jesus is apparently the Gospel; other views identify it as the Torah or both scriptures.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه الإنجيل وقيل التوراة وقيل مجموعهما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses blessed as beneficial, including healing the blind and leprous.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد نفاعا ومن نفعه إبراء الأكمه والأبرص

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān says Jesus benefited others by teaching good, commanding right, and forbidding wrong.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان : معلم الخير آمر بالمعروف ناهيا عن المنكر

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk interprets blessed as one who meets people's needs; the author prefers Mujāhid's broader ‘beneficial’ sense.
rows.anchor: وعن الضحاك قاضيا للحوائج والأول أولى لعمومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past-tense verbs describe either what was fixed by God's decree or what was certain to occur as though already completed; al-Ḥasan reports that Jesus was given full reason and prophethood as a child.
rows.anchor: والتعبير بلفظ الماضي في الأفعال الثلاثة إما باعتبار ما في القضاء المحتوم

rows.speaker: أنس؛ ابن أبي حاتم
rows.claim: Anas reports that Jesus studied and mastered the Gospel in his mother's womb, explaining his statement that he was given the book.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن أنس أن عيسى عليه السلام درس الإنجيل وأحكمه في بطن أمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aynamā kuntu is conditional, with its omitted consequence ‘He made me blessed’ supplied from the preceding words; the condition cannot grammatically be governed by the earlier jaʿalanī.
rows.anchor: وفي البحران هذا شرط وجزاؤه محذوف تقديره جعلني مباركا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakat is variously explained as the obligatory alms-tax or, with prayer as supplication, purification of the soul; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh's argument that prophets have no zakat is questioned.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بالصلاة الدعاء وبالزكاة تطهير النفس عن الرذائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The esoteric reading is not necessary: on the apparent sense, Jesus may be commanded to institute zakat for his community, or to pay wealth-zakat if he owns wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا يتعين لأن ذلك أمر له بإيجاب الزكاة على أمته وهو خلاف الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘as long as I live’ ordinarily means Jesus' life in this world, not his time in heaven; extending it to heavenly life would also entail prayer there.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن الظاهر المتبادر من المدة المذكورة مدة كونه عليه الصلاة والسلام حيا في الدنيا

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة؛ ابن كثير؛ أبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers are reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya to read dumtu with kasra on the dāl; the author has not found the reading in other sources and notes that it is called a dialect form.
rows.anchor: ونقل ابن عطية أن أهل المدينة وابن كثير وأبا عمرو قرأوا ( دمت ) بكسر الدال

rows.speaker: الحوفي؛ أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ connect ‘dutiful to my mother’ to ‘blessed’; Abū Ḥayyān objects to the distance created by the intervening clause and prefers an implied ‘He made me dutiful.’
rows.anchor: عطف على ( مباركا ) على ما قال الحوفي وأبو البقاء وتعقبه أبو حيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This statement strongly suggests Jesus had no father and is the clearest indication in the passage of Mary's innocence.
rows.anchor: قيل هذا كالصريح في أنه عليه السلام لا والد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra reading of barran may be parsed as a personal quality, an implied verb meaning ‘obliged me,’ or a complement of awṣānī; the author finds ‘obliged me’ more apt than the poetic analogy of supplying food and cold water.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون النصب بفعل في معنى ( أوصاني ) أي وألزمني أو وكلفني برا

rows.speaker: الزهراوي؛ أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawī and Abū al-Baqāʾ transmit barrin with kasra and tanwīn, coordinated directly with prayer and zakat; the tanwīn magnifies the quality.
rows.anchor: وحكى الزهراوي وأبو البقاء أنه قريء ( وبر ) بكسر الباء والراذ وهو معطوف على الصلاة والزكاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God did not decree Jesus to be arrogant and wretched; he lived humbly, ate leaves, wore wool, sat on earth, and kept no home.
rows.anchor: وقد كان عليه السلام في غاية التواضع يأكل الشجر ويلبس الشعر ويجلس على التراب

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: Jesus is reported to have said, ‘Ask me, for I am tenderhearted and small in my own estimation.’
rows.anchor: وكان عليه السلام يقول : سلوني فإني لين القلب صغير في نفسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-salām is generic peace, implicitly cursing Mary's accusers: if all peace is assigned to Jesus, its opposite is being wished on his enemies. The apparent reading as a definite, previously mentioned peace is unlikely and misses the polemical insinuation.
rows.anchor: والأظهر بل الصحيح أن التغريب للجنس جيء به تعريضا باللعنة على متهمي مريم وأعدائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison ‘peace upon the one who follows guidance’ means punishment for the one who denies and turns away (20:47); the context is one of dispute and hostility.
rows.anchor: ونظيره قوله تعالى ( والسلام على من اتبع الهدى ) يعني أن العذاب على من كذب وتولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Identifying an antecedent from John’s peace fails because the passage is separate in narrative and sense; assigning peace by generic usage better creates the contrast required by the context.
rows.anchor: لأن هذا الكلام منقطع عن ذلك وجودا وسدرا فيكون معهودا غير سابق لفظا ومعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes John's greeting stronger because God spoke it; another makes Jesus' stronger because God places Jesus in His own position and gives him exclusive peace, a comparison left for reflection.
rows.anchor: وقيل هذا أرجح لما فيه من إقامة الله تعالى إياه في ذلك مقام نفسه

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī reads waladtu with feminine tāʾ, making the verb agree with Jesus' mother.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما ( يوم ولدت ) بتاء التأنيث وإسناد الفعل إلى والدته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālika points to Jesus with his noble attributes, elevating him, setting him apart, and making him seem present to the listener; ‘son of Mary’ can be an adjective, a second predicate, apposition, or explanatory substitute, with adjective most common.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى من فصلت نعوته الجليلة وفيه إشارة إلى علو رتبته وبعد منزلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage identifies Jesus as God's servant and Mary's son, not as Christians describe him, refuting their claim by explicitly naming the contrary attributes; the exclusion follows from the context.
rows.anchor: والمراد ذلك هو عيسى ابن مريم لا ما يصفه النصارى وهو تكذيب لهم على الوجه الأبلغ

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī says definiteness of both subject and predicate itself gives an exclusive sense; the author finds this account less convincing than the contextual implication.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو مستفاد من تعريف الطرفين بناء على ما ذكره الكرماني من أن تعريفهما مطلقا يفيد الحصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qawl al-ḥaqq can be an accusative of praise, a circumstantial phrase, a direct verbal noun meaning ‘I say the truth,’ or an emphatic verbal noun with an omitted governing word; al-Ḥaqq may mean God or His word ‘Be.’
rows.anchor: نصب على المدح والمراد بالحق الله تعالى وبالقول كلمته تعالى

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: The author reports the view that qawl al-ḥaqq emphatically confirms Jesus' preceding declaration, ‘I am God's servant.’
rows.anchor: وقال شيخ الإسلام : هو مصدر مؤكد لقال إني عبد الله

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read qawlu in the nominative as a predicate of an omitted subject, a description of Jesus, or apposition; each makes the phrase God's true word.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور ( قول ) بالرفع على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هو قول الحق

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود؛ الحسن؛ طلحة؛ الأعمش
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads qāla al-ḥaqq; al-Ḥasan uses a variant vocalization of qawl; Ṭalḥa and al-Aʿmash read qāla al-ḥaqq as a verb with al-ḥaqq its subject. Another reading has qāla Allāh.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود ( قال الحق ) وقال الله برفع ( قال ) فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disputants over Jesus include Jews who call him a sorcerer and Christians who call him God's son; the author rejects both claims.
rows.anchor: فيقول اليهود : هو ساحر وحاشاه ويقول النصارى : ابن الله سبحان الله عما يقولون

rows.speaker: علي؛ السلمي؛ داود بن أبي هند؛ نافع؛ الكسائي
rows.claim: These readers have tamtarūna with second-person tāʾ, directly addressing those who dispute the matter.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه والسلمي وداود بن أبي هند ونافع في رواية والكسائي كذلك ( تمترون ) بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God cannot rightly or fittingly take a child; the verse refutes the Christians and declares God exalted above their fabrication.
rows.anchor: ما صح وما استقام له جل شأنه اتخاذ ذلك وهو تكذيب للنصارى وتنزيه له عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's immediate creative command rebukes the idea of a child: one who brings anything into being instantly has no need for offspring, which would imply need or deficiency.
rows.anchor: تبكيت له ببيان أن شأنه إذا قضى أمرا من الأمور أو يوجد بأسرع وقت

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads fa-yakūna in the accusative as a subjunctive response to the command kun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر ( فيكون ) بالنصب على الجواب

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī connects ‘God is my Lord and yours’ to Jesus' declaration ‘I am God's servant,’ making it a continuation of his speech; the two verses are parenthetical, supported by Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ubayy omits the conjunction.
rows.anchor: عطف على ما قال الواحدي على قوله ( إني عبد الله ) فهو من تمام قول عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, the verse is apparently addressed through an implied command to Muhammad: say that God is my Lord and yours.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه على هذا بتقدير خطابا لسيد المخاطبين صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الخليل؛ سيبويه؛ الزمخشري
rows.claim: The reading wa-anna with open hamza is explained by deleting a preposition and attaching the clause to faʿbudūhu, as in the declaration that mosques belong to God (72:18).
rows.anchor: وخرجه الزمخشري على حذف حرف الجر وتعلقه باعبدوه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows the clause to be a verbal noun coordinated with ‘zakat,’ meaning Jesus was also charged to affirm that God is Lord of all.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الفراء أن يكون أن وما بعدها في تأويل مصدر عطفا على ( الزكاة )

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī parses the clause as the predicate of an omitted subject: ‘the matter is that God is my Lord and yours.’
rows.anchor: وأجاز الكسائي أن يكون ذلك خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي والأمر أن الله ربي وربكم

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء؛ أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: A reported Abū ʿAmr analysis coordinates the clause with ‘a matter’ in the prior verse; the author calls this grammatical confusion and doubts the report, while also noting coordination with ‘the book.’
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو عبيدة عن أبي عمرو بن العلاء أنه عطف على ( أمرا ) من قوله تعالى ( إذا قضى أمرا )

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy's variant wa-bi-an has a conjunction and preposition; it is attached either to prayer or zakat or to the command to worship.
rows.anchor: وفي حرف أبي رضي الله تعالى عنه أيضا ( وبأن ) بالواو وباء الجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to worship God addresses Jesus' contemporaries or Muhammad's; tawḥīd is the straight path from which the traveler does not stray.
rows.anchor: والخطاب إما لمعاصري عيسى عليه السلام وإما لمعاصري نبينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transition shows the parties making what should unite them—the clear testimony that Jesus is God's servant and messenger—the source of division through excess and neglect.
rows.anchor: تنبيها على سوء صنيعهم بجعلهم ما يوجب الاتفاق منشأ للاختلاف

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī identifies the disputing parties as Jews and Christians; min baynihim stresses that the division arose among the very people named.
rows.anchor: فالمراد بالأحزاب اليهود والنصارى وهو المروي عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other grammatical explanations take min as extra or bayn as ‘distance,’ making their disagreement result from distance from truth; the latter is remote.
rows.anchor: ونقل في البحر القول بزيادة من وحكى أيضا القول بأن البين هنا بمعنى البعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view limits the parties to Christian sects after Jesus' ascension: Nestorius made him God's son, Jacob said he was God, and Melkites called him God's servant and prophet while teaching the union of divine and human natures.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بالأحزاب فرق النصارى فإنهم اختلفوابعد رفعه عليه السلام فيه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the parties are those who conspired against the prophets and then disputed over Jesus after his story was recited to them.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أنهم الذين تحزبوا على الأنبياء عليهم الصلاة والسلام لما قص عليهم قصة عيسى

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: A view that the parties are all disbelievers, including Jews, Christians, and others, is preferred by the Imam because the wording contains no restriction; the immediate context also favors the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: قيل : إنهم مطلق الكفار فيشمل اليهود والنصارى والمشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the parties disbelievers signals that all are unbelievers and explains their condemnation; if Muslims or Melkites are included among the parties, the warning applies only to their disbelieving faction.
rows.anchor: فالمراد بهم الأحزاب المختلفون وعبر عنهم بذلك إيذانا بكفرهم جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘great day’ is the Day of Resurrection and judgment; it may mean the witnessed event, its time or place, or the testimony against them by angels, prophets, tongues, and limbs.
rows.anchor: وهو يوم القيامة أو من وقت شهوده أو مكان الشهود فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views take the great spectacle as the parties' statement about Jesus and his mother, likened to a grave utterance, or as the day believers were killed; the latter is remote.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو ماشهدوا به في حق عيسى عليه السلام وأمه وعظمه لعظم ما فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that the threatened day is the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: والحق أن المراد بذلك اليوم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الحسن؛ قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda explain the exclamation as amazement at how keenly the people will hear and see on Judgment Day, after being deaf and blind in worldly life.
rows.anchor: تعجيب من حدة سمعهم وأبصارهم يومئذ ومعناه أن أسماعهم وأبصارهم

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā reads the expression as a threat: they will hear what tears at their hearts and see what blackens their faces.
rows.anchor: هو وعيد وتهديد أي سوف يسمعون ما يخلع قلوبهم ويبصرون ما يسود وجوههم

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya takes it as an actual command to the Messenger to make them hear and see the promises and punishments of that day.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي العالية أنه أمر حقيقة للرسول ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) بأن يسمعهم ويبصرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under the amazement readings, the prepositional phrase is conventionally parsed in the nominative; under the literal imperative, it is accusative, with an obligatory implied subject.
rows.anchor: والجار والمجرور على الأولين في موضع الرفع على القول المشهور وعلى الأخير في محل نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Today’ means worldly life: wrongdoers have plainly lost their way by wholly neglecting to listen and look, and they are called wrongdoers to expose their self-injury.
rows.anchor: لا يدرك غايته حيث اغفلوا الأستماع والنظر بالكلية ووضع ( الظالمين ) موضع الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Abū al-ʿĀliya's imperative reading, the warning is a parenthetical clarification of the preceding threat against the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: والأستدراك على ما نقل عن أبي العالية يتعلق بقوله تعالى ( فويل للذين كفروا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is apparently directed to the wrongdoers; Abū Ḥayyān says it addresses all people. The Day of Regret is when wrongdoers lament their neglect of God's claims, while the righteous regret too little good.
rows.anchor: أي الظالمين على ما هو الظاهر وقال أبو حيان : الضمير لجميع الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the matter is settled may mean reckoning ends, the people enter Paradise or Hell, death is slaughtered, and each group is told it will remain forever; al-Suddī and Ibn Jurayj mention only death's slaughter.
rows.anchor: أي فرغ من الحساب وذهب أهل الجنة إلى الجنة وأهل النار إلى النار وذبح الموت

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد؛ النبي
rows.claim: A report in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and al-Tirmidhī says death appears as a white-black ram, is recognized by both groups, and is slaughtered between Paradise and Hell; then each hears it will have no more death.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سعيد قال : قال رسول الله ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) يؤتى بالموت كهيئة كبش أملح

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says disbelievers' regret comes when they see the places they would have occupied in Paradise had they believed.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية عن ابن مسعود أن يوم الحسرة حين يرى الكفار مقاعدهم من الجنة لو كانوا مؤمنين

rows.speaker: الضحاك؛ ابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk locates the regret when Hell emerges and hurls sparks; Ibn Zayd takes the Day of Regret as Judgment Day generally, containing regrets at many stages.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك : ذلك إذا برزت جهنم ورمت بالشر وقيل : المراد بذلك يوم القيامة مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generic sense of regret includes the losses described, regret when records are received in the left hands, and other occasions; settling the matter may mean the end of worldly life.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قيل : المراد بالحسرة جنسها فيشمل ذلك حسرتهم فيما ذكر وحسرتهم عند أخذ الكتب بالشمائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning, supported by the preceding report, is the day death is slaughtered and eternal life announced, the greatest regret because hope ends and escape closes.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن ظاهر الحديث السابق وكذا غيره كما لا يخفى على المتتبع قاض بأن يوم الحسرة يوم يذبح الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unusual claim that settlement means repentance's door closes when the sun rises in the west is rejected as pointless.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب ما قيل : إن المراد بقضاء المر سد باب التوبة حين تطلع الشمس من مغربها وليس بشيئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the other readings, idh is either appositional to ‘day’ or governed by al-ḥasra, whose definite verbal noun can take a temporal object.
rows.anchor: و ( إذ ) على سائر الأقوال بدل من ( يوم ) أو متعلق بالحسرة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري؛ الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī, transmitting from al-Ḥasan, attaches ‘while they are heedless and do not believe’ to ‘in clear error’ as two circumstantial clauses; al-Kashf prefers coordination with the statement that wrongdoers are astray.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري : متعلق بقوله تعالى شأنه ( في ضلال مبين ) عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred syntax coordinates the clauses with ‘the wrongdoers are in clear error,’ while ‘warn them’ is parenthetical and stresses their heedlessness.
rows.anchor: واستظهر في الكشف العطف على قوله تعالى : ( الظالمون في ضلال مبين )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parsing makes the clauses circumstances of those being warned; although one may object that warning the heedless conflicts with warning only those who fear, the author says warning also awakens people to their afterlife interests.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون ذلك متعلقا بأنذارهم على أنه حال من المفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection is not decisive: warnings can remind heedless people, as in ‘remind, for the reminder benefits believers’ (51:55), and the repeated Qur'anic mission is to warn an unaware people; the Messenger must convey.
rows.anchor: وذكر فإن الذكرى تنفع المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God inherits the earth when no other ownership remains; everything then belongs to Him openly and inwardly, as in ‘To whom belongs sovereignty today? To God’ (40:16).
rows.anchor: لا يبقى لأحد غيره تعالى ملك ولا ملك فيكون كل ذلك له تعالى استقلالا ظاهرا وباطنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God takes the earth and its inhabitants through destruction, as an heir takes an inheritance into possession.
rows.anchor: أو نتوفى الأرض ومن عليها بالإفناء والإهلاك توفى الوارث لارثه واستيفائه إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All return to God for recompense, not independently or jointly to anyone else.
rows.anchor: أي يردون إلى الجزاء لا إالى غيرنا استقلالا أو اشتراكا

rows.speaker: الأعرج؛ السلمي؛ ابن إسحاق؛ عيسى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraj reads the return verb with tāʾ; al-Sulamī, Ibn Isḥāq, and ʿĪsā read it with yāʾ in the active voice, though al-Dānī reports their tāʾ form too.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعرج ( ترجعون ) بالتاء الفوقية وقرأ السلمى وابن إسحاق وعيسى بالياء التحتية مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an allusive interpretation, the opening letters kāf-hā-yā-ʿayn-ṣād are, correctly, among God's hidden secrets; another allegory assigns each letter a divine name corresponding to Zechariah's weakness, need for guidance and protection, hidden causes, and God's fulfilled promise.
rows.anchor: هو وأمثاله على الصحيح سر من أسرار الله تعالى وقيل في وجه افتتاح هذه السورة به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two stories allusively teach that God grants gifts both when asked and without a request; allegorical mappings onto the inner self are criticized as strained.
rows.anchor: والأشارة في القصتين اجمالا إلى أن الله تعالى شأنه يهب بسؤال وغير سؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vow of silence alludes to abandoning self-defense: Mary is told to keep silent, showing God's power, and God vindicates her by making Jesus speak.
rows.anchor: وفي نذر الصوم والمراد به الصمت اشارة إلى ترك الانتصار للنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some mystics say ‘I am God's servant’ gathers every noble attribute; being God's servant is greater praise than the bare word, though this station is especially associated with Muhammad, with a qualification about the word not being joined to divine knowledge.
rows.anchor: وذكر أنه عليه السلام طوى كل وصف جميل في مطاوى قوله ( إني عبد الله )

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ defines the arrogant person as one who does not advise others and the wretched person as one who will not accept advice, and seeks God's protection from both.
rows.anchor: وذكر ابن عطاء في قوله تعالى ( ولم يجعلني جبارا شقيا ) أن الجبار الذي لا ينصح والشقي الذي لا ينتصح

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd connects ‘remember’ to the command to warn; another view attaches it to the earlier ‘remember,’ which the author finds more apparent.
rows.anchor: عطف على ( أنذرهم ) عند أبي السعود وقيل : على اذكر السابق ولعله الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘In the Book’ means this sūrah or the Qur'an; ‘remember Abraham’ means recite his story to people, as in the command to recite his account (26:69).
rows.anchor: أي هذه السورة أو في القرآن ( إبراهيم ( أي اتل على الناس قصته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although al-Kashshāf says God is the one remembering Abraham in the Book, the Prophet counts as doing so because he speaks for God and conveys His command.
rows.anchor: والافذاكر ذلك في الكتاب هو الله تعالى كما في الكشاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's story follows the refutation of those who deify Jesus: it also condemns worship of an inanimate object, while both groups err and the second is more deeply astray.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها اشتمالها على تضليل من نسب الالوهية إلى الجماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ‘remember’ is linked to ‘warn them,’ Abraham's story may persuade people who claim descent from him to abandon their wrongs.
rows.anchor: فانهم ينتمون اليه ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) فعساهم باستماع قصته يقلعون عماهم فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣiddīq means constant truthfulness and nabiy is a second predicate; this ordering keeps the first quality from seeming restricted to prophets, since every prophet is truthful.
rows.anchor: أي ملازم الصدق لم يكذب قط ( نبيا

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf treats ṣiddīq as an intensive form: Abraham's abundant belief in divine mysteries, signs, books, and messengers outweighed other forms of belief, while he was himself a prophet.
rows.anchor: الصديق من أبنية المبالغة والمراد فرط صدقه وكثرة ما صدق به من غيوب الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intensity may concern the quantity or quality of truthfulness, or both; the author rejects counting multiplication of objects as the relevant grammatical intensification and prefers derivation from ṣidq rather than taṣdīq.
rows.anchor: واستظهر أنه من الصدق لا من التصديق وأيد بأنه قرئ ( انه كان صادقا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret prophet here as one of high rank before God and people.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم النبي هنا برفيع القدر عند الله تعالى وعند الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle idh has been attached to Abraham as an appositional substitute, but objections say an uncoordinated substitute is unnatural and idh is usually indeclinable; other proposals attach it to kāna, prophet, or ṣiddīq, each with grammatical or contextual problems.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه صاحب الفرائد بأن الأعتراض بين البدل والمبدل منه بدون الواو بعيد عن الطبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best account makes idh an appositional substitute of inclusion for Abraham; attaching remembrance to times rather than events has been explained elsewhere.
rows.anchor: والذي يقتضيه السياق ويشهد به الذوق البدلية وهو بدل اشتمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā abati means ‘my father’: tāʾ replaces the possessive yāʾ, which is not normally combined with it except rarely; the added alif has competing grammatical explanations.
rows.anchor: يا أبت ( أي يا أبي فان التاء عوض من ياء الأضافه ولذلك لايجمع بينهما إلا شذوذا

rows.speaker: ابن عامر؛ الأعرج؛ أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿraj, and Abū Jaʿfar read the vocative with fatḥa on tāʾ; Hārūn calls it incorrect, but the author says it is valid. ʿAbd Allāh's codex has wāw instead of yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر والأعرج وابو جعفر ( يا أبت ) بفتح التاء وزعم هارون أن ذلك لحن والحق خلافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham uses the affectionate vocative to soften his appeal.
rows.anchor: وناداه عليه السلام بذلك استعطافاله

rows.speaker: أنس؛ أبو نعيم؛ الديلمي
rows.claim: A report raised to the Prophet says a child should address his father as Abraham addressed his—‘my father’—and not call him by name; this appears to imply biological fatherhood, though many hold that Abraham's addressee was his uncle and ‘father’ figurative.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو نعيم والدليمي عن انس مرفوعا حق الوالد على ولده أن لا يسميه إلا بما سمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What you worship’ means an object that cannot hear your praise and appeals or cannot see your humility; alternatively, it cannot hear or see any sensible thing at all. Mā may be relative or an indefinite described noun.
rows.anchor: ثناءك عليه عند عبادتك له وجؤارك اليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘It cannot avail you anything’ means it cannot bring benefit; shayʾan may be a direct object or an accusative verbal noun.
rows.anchor: من الأشياء أو شيئا من الأغناء فهو نصب على المفعولية أتو المصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's argument models the finest method and manners: he asks for the reason behind worshiping something any rational person despises, avoiding a provocation to stubbornness while showing that worship belongs only to the self-sufficient creator and judge.
rows.anchor: ولقد سلك عليه السلام في دعوته أحسن منهاج واحتج عليه أبد احتجاج بحسن أدب وخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rational person should act for a sound reason; even a living, perceptive being capable of benefit and harm would be dependent and unfit for worship, much less a lifeless manufactured idol.
rows.anchor: والشيئ لو كان حيا مميزا سميعا بصيرا قادرا على النفع والضر لكن كان ممكنا لاستنكف ذو العقل السليم عن عبادته
